c.tagline: The Alamo City — Spanish missions, the winding River Walk, and Tex-Mex under the Texas sun.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis charge roughly $24-29 for a downtown-to-airport trip. Uber and Lyft operate citywide and are usually cheaper and easier to find than a street taxi.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 311 is the non-emergency city line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Downtown / River Walk: the Alamo mission and the cypress-lined River Walk promenade
hood_landmark.Southtown: the Blue Star Arts Complex and its First Friday gallery nights
hood_landmark.Pearl District: the restored Pearl Brewery complex with its weekend farmers market
hood_landmark.Alamo Heights: the McNay Art Museum in its Spanish Colonial-style mansion and grounds

avoid.reason: Downtown blocks away from the River Walk empty out at night — watch for petty theft and car break-ins, and keep usual awareness around the bus station area late.

hood_desc: San Antonio's tourist core, home to the Alamo, the winding River Walk (Paseo del Río) lined with restaurants and cantinas, La Villita, the Tower of the Americas, and the Majestic Theatre; the classic first-timer base, walkable and connected by river barge.

A lively arts district just south of downtown centered on the Blue Star Arts Complex and South Alamo Street, with galleries, murals, indie cafes, taquerias, and the monthly First Friday art walk; popular with a young creative crowd.

A revitalized former brewery on the northern edge of downtown, now a stylish food-and-culture hub with Hotel Emma, a weekend farmers market, top restaurants, boutiques, and the Culinary Institute of America campus.

An affluent, established area north of downtown with tree-lined streets, the McNay Art Museum, Brackenridge Park and the San Antonio Zoo nearby, and upscale shopping at the Quarry; quiet and family-friendly.
lodging: Drury Inn & Suites San Antonio Riverwalk
Hyatt Place San Antonio Airport/Quarry Market

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: VIA buses run roughly 5:00 AM to midnight on major routes, with reduced frequency evenings and Sundays; outlying service is sparse, so most visitors rely on ride-hail or a rental car beyond downtown.
transit.note: San Antonio is car-oriented and spread out; the downtown River Walk core is very walkable, but VIA bus service to the missions or the airport is slow, so Uber, Lyft, or a rental car are the practical choices.
transit.pay: Pay onboard with cash (exact $1.30 base fare), the VIA goMobile+ app, or a reloadable VIA card; a day pass is about $2.75. Most routes converge on Centro Plaza and the downtown transit centers.

car.idp: Not required (US and most foreign licenses accepted)

train: Amtrak Sunset Limited & Texas Eagle (downtown San Antonio station)

transit.m: VIA Route 5 bus to downtown (~40 min)
Uber or Lyft to downtown (~15 min)

tip.r: ~18-20% at restaurants; $1-2 per drink at bars and ~15% for taxi rides.

food.name: Puffy tacos
food.desc: A masa tortilla pressed and dropped into hot oil so it balloons, then folded around picadillo or beans. San Antonio's own invention.

places.name: Henry's Puffy Tacos
places.note: Crisp-outside, chewy-inside shell widely rated the city's best; family-run for decades.

places.name: Ray's Drive Inn
places.note: 1956 drive-in that claims to have named the puffy taco; a genuine local shrine.

places.name: Los Barrios Mexican Restaurant
places.note: Long-running Blanco Road Tex-Mex room; puffy tacos plus strong margaritas.

food.name: Breakfast tacos
food.desc: Warm flour tortillas folded around eggs with bean, potato, chorizo or bacon. Cheap, early and the subject of civic pride here.

places.name: Taco Haven
places.note: Neighbourhood counter open since 1971; regulars queue before 8am for the migas.

places.name: Rolando's Super Tacos
places.note: Eggs cooked to order and the enormous El Gigante taco; cash-friendly and fast.

places.name: Panchito's Mexican Restaurant
places.note: Reliable all-day tacos on flour tortillas made in house.

food.name: Barbacoa
food.desc: Slow-steamed beef cheek, rich and gelatinous, scooped into tortillas on Sunday mornings. Locally inseparable from a bottle of Big Red.

places.name: Tellez Tamales and Barbacoa
places.note: Weekend-morning institution; go early, the barbacoa sells out.

places.name: Mi Tierra Cafe y Panaderia
places.note: Open 24 hours since 1941, so barbacoa is available at any hour.

places.name: Anacacho at the St. Anthony Hotel
places.note: Polished hotel-cafe version of the Big Red and barbacoa pairing.

food.name: Pan dulce
food.desc: Mexican sweet breads from the panaderia case: sugar-crusted conchas, cuernos and empanadas, taken with coffee or after barbacoa.

places.name: Mi Tierra Cafe y Panaderia
places.note: Vast bakery counter under the famous mural; tray-and-tongs self service.

places.name: La Panaderia
places.note: Mexico City brothers baking conchas and pan dulce with serious technique.

places.name: Panifico Bake Shop
places.note: Neighbourhood bakery known for conchas and cafe de olla.

food.name: Chili con carne
food.desc: The bowl of red that San Antonio's Chili Queens sold on the plazas in the 1800s: beef and chile, no beans, cornbread on the side.

places.name: Mi Tierra Cafe y Panaderia
places.note: Serves it near the plazas where the Chili Queens once set up their tables.

places.name: Schilo's Delicatessen
places.note: German-Texan deli from 1917; old-school bowl of red and house root beer.

places.name: Boudro's Texas Bistro
places.note: Upscale Texas cooking on the river; strong Southwestern menu and famous guacamole.

food.name: Cheese enchiladas
food.desc: The Tex-Mex combination plate anchor: corn tortillas rolled around cheese and onion, drowned in chili gravy with rice and refried beans.

places.name: Los Barrios Mexican Restaurant
places.note: Family recipes since 1979; the combination plate is the thing to order.

places.name: La Fonda on Main
places.note: Open since 1932 with a shaded patio; the city's oldest Mexican restaurant.

places.name: Rosario's Mexican Cafe y Cantina
places.note: Bright, loud Southtown room; interior Mexican dishes plus full Tex-Mex.

food.name: Big Red
food.desc: Bright red cream soda invented in Texas and drunk ice-cold with barbacoa on Sunday morning. A local pairing bordering on ritual.

places.name: Tellez Tamales and Barbacoa
places.note: The definitive barbacoa-and-Big-Red weekend combination.

places.name: Mi Tierra Cafe y Panaderia
places.note: Always in the cooler; pairs it with barbacoa around the clock.

places.name: Henry's Puffy Tacos
places.note: Standard drink alongside the puffy tacos and breakfast plates.

food.name: Prickly pear margarita
food.desc: Tequila and lime shaded magenta with syrup from the fruit of the Texas nopal cactus. Tart, floral and everywhere along the river.

places.name: Boudro's Texas Bistro
places.note: Its prickly pear margarita is the city's best-known cocktail.

places.name: Rosario's Mexican Cafe y Cantina
places.note: Big cantina bar with fruit-forward margaritas and a First Friday crowd.

places.name: The Esquire Tavern
places.note: Texas's longest wooden bar, open since 1933; serious cocktail programme.

landmarks: The Alamo
The 1718 mission-turned-fortress where Texan defenders made their legendary 1836 last stand remains America's most storied shrine to independence.
San Antonio River Walk
Stone footpaths, arched bridges and cypress-shaded cafes line this winding urban canal, best savoured from a slow-gliding river barge.
Mission San José
The 'Queen of the Missions', a UNESCO-listed 1720 complex whose carved Rose Window is the finest Spanish-colonial ornament in the United States.
Mission Concepción
America's oldest unrestored stone church still shows traces of original frescoes on walls that have stood since 1755.
San Fernando Cathedral
Founded in 1731 and among the nation's oldest cathedrals, its facade becomes the canvas for a dazzling nightly video-art projection.
Tower of the Americas
This 750-foot spire from the 1968 World's Fair crowns Hemisfair with revolving-restaurant views stretching across the Texas Hill Country.
Historic Market Square (El Mercado)
The largest Mexican market north of the border pulses with mariachis, folk-art stalls and the famous pastries of Mi Tierra cafe.
The Pearl District
A riverside brewery reborn as San Antonio's hippest quarter, packed with acclaimed restaurants, a weekend farmers market and the Hotel Emma.
Japanese Tea Garden
A century-old quarry transformed into stone bridges, koi ponds and a 60-foot waterfall beneath a pagoda-style pavilion in Brackenridge Park.
McNay Art Museum
Texas's first modern-art museum fills a Spanish-Colonial mansion and its rose gardens with works by Picasso, O'Keeffe and Matisse.

train.note: No passenger trains cross the border from Texas - Mexico's national passenger network does not connect here. Amtrak's daily Texas Eagle (north to Austin, Dallas, Little Rock and Chicago) and the thrice-weekly Sunset Limited (east to Houston and New Orleans, west to El Paso, Tucson and Los Angeles) call at the downtown station at 350 Hobart Street beside the Alamodome. The two trains run combined west of San Antonio, and the Sunset Limited passes through in the small hours, so check departure times carefully. Coaches to Austin are faster, cheaper and far more frequent than the train.

intl.to: Monterrey, Nuevo Laredo & other Mexican cities

bus.note: Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) run frequent domestic coaches from the downtown station on N St Mary's Street to Austin in about 1.5 hours, Houston in 3.5 and Dallas in 5, with fares from a few dollars if booked early. Tornado Bus and Turimex Internacional run cross-border services to Monterrey and beyond from their own terminals west of downtown; carry your passport, and expect to leave the bus at Laredo for both US and Mexican immigration checks. Travel beyond the Mexican border zone also needs an FMM tourist card, issued at the crossing.

ferry.note: San Antonio is landlocked and has no ferry services. The River Walk barges are sightseeing and short-hop shuttle boats within downtown only, and the nearest coast is at Corpus Christi, about two hours away by road.
